title: Searching for Axion Dark Matter via Superconductor-Spin Hybrid Magnetometers
authors: Runqi Kang, Jian Zhang, Liangliang Rong, Xing Rong
abstract: Axions are a compelling dark matter candidate suggested by theories beyond the Standard Model. The predicted axion-electron coupling and the resulting pseudomagnetic field allow for laboratory axion searches. Here we report an experimental axion search via a superconductor-spin hybrid magnetometer. A state-of-the-art broadband magnetometer with a sensitivity of sub-100 aT/Hz$^{1/2}$ at tens of kHz has been realized by coupling a ferrite spin sensor to a readout system based on a superconducting quantum interference device. The most stringent terrestrial constraints on the axion-electron coupling have been established in the frequency range 5$\sim$60 kHz. In the future, an improvement on the constraints of more than 4 orders of magnitude is foreseeable through arrays of superconductor-spin hybrid magnetometers with optimized designs. This work demonstrates the potential of superconductor-spin hybrid magnetometers in high-precision magnetic field sensing and the study of fundamental physics.
summary: This work reports on an experimental search for Axion Dark Matter using a highly sensitive superconductor-spin hybrid magnetometer. By coupling a spin sensor (ferrite) to a SQUID readout, the authors achieved state-of-the-art magnetic field sensitivity in the tens of kHz range. The results set new, stringent upper limits on the axion-electron coupling constant, advancing the field of fundamental physics detection.
main_problem: The primary goal is the experimental search for Axion Dark Matter, a compelling candidate predicted by theories beyond the Standard Model.
main_result: The experiment established the most stringent terrestrial constraints on the axion-electron coupling in the 5–60 kHz frequency range, rejecting all tested axion hypotheses.
method: The search utilizes a novel superconductor-spin hybrid magnetometer to detect the minute pseudomagnetic field generated by ambient axion dark matter.
model_or_system: The system comprises a high-permeability MnZn ferrite rod containing electron spins, coupled to a Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) readout system, all housed in a dilution refrigerator.
key_observables: Power Excess (PE) spectra, magnetic flux ($\Phi_{in}$), and the derived upper bounds on the axion-electron coupling constant ($g_{aee}$).
important_parameters: Sensitivity achieved sub-100 aT/Hz$^{1/2}$ at tens of kHz; the search is constrained in the 5–60 kHz frequency range.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the axion signal couples to the MnZn ferrite spins, and that the signal must be consistent across multiple independent measurement runs.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, calibration of the magnetometer's gain and sensitivity, the processed power excess spectra from multiple runs, and the final constraint plot showing the derived upper bounds on $g_{aee}$ versus frequency.
paper_structure: The paper details the theoretical motivation (axion coupling), the experimental platform (hybrid magnetometer), the detailed calibration procedures (measuring permeability and sensitivity), the data analysis pipeline (power spectrum extraction and averaging), and finally, the presentation of the derived constraints on the axion coupling.
why_interesting: While the primary focus is particle astrophysics, the core technology relies on ultra-sensitive magnetic field sensing using superconducting circuits coupled to quantum materials (ferrites/spins), which touches upon advanced quantum sensing techniques relevant to AMO physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Experimental setup and circuit model for the SQUID. (a) The superconductor-spin hybrid system. A SQUID and a spin-based magnetic-field amplifier made of MnZn ferrite were placed in a magnetic shield and a vacuum chamber. The SQUID and the amplifier were coupled via a superconducting coil. (b) Circuit model for the SQUID. The axion-induced magnetic flux was transferred to the SQUID loop through a coupling circuit. The SQUID loop was biased by a DC current and traduce the magnetic flux into a voltage signal.

FIG. 2. Calibration results. (a) Relative permeability and gain. The measured relative permeability µr of the MnZn ferrite is shown as black circles. For every value for µr, the gain of the magnetic-field amplifier can be obtained through finite-element simulation, as the red triangles shows. The lines are interpolations of the data points. (b) Sensitivity of the superconductor-spin hybrid magnetometer to a real magnetic field. The noise floor is below 100 aT/Hz1/2 (the red dashed line). Peaks in the spectrum are attributed to noise leakage from the environment.

FIG. 4. (a) Constraints on the axion-electron coupling as a function of the frequency and the axion mass. Our experimental results are shown as the blue solid line. The yellow and gray regions are the parameter spaces excluded by previous haloscopes [19–22] and a fifth-force experiment [24], respectively. Astronomy limits on stellar axions are shown as the gray dotted line. With future optimization in the design and increase in the number of setups, our constraints can be improved by more than four orders of magnitude, as the blue dashed line shows. (b) Zoom-in of the frequency range 5∼60 kHz.

FIG. 3. Results of Run 1. (a) One filtered PE spectrum of Run 1. (b) Average standardized power excesses. The gray dots are data points and the blue bars are counting results. 1728 data points exceed the threshold for an axion hypothesis. They are rejected in succeeding runs.
FIG. 5. (a) Measured Mc in the frequency range from 1 kHz to 60 kHz. (b) Dependence of Mc and G on the relative permeability.
